turns.content: Let `n = 2022`. Lucy may add two previously written integer `n`-tuples or take their coordinatewise maximum. Consider the three starting tuples `a_i = -i^2`, `b_i = i`, and `c_i = -1`. For fixed `j`, form `d^(j) = 2a + 4j b + (2j^2 - 1)c`. Explain why it is obtainable and compute its `i`-th coordinate.
Use the formula for `d^(j)_i` to determine its value when `i = j` and its bound when `i != j`. What tuple is obtained by taking the coordinatewise maximum of `d^(1), ..., d^(n)`?
Starting from that all-ones tuple and `c`, construct the zero tuple. Then show how `d^(j)` and the zero tuple produce the standard basis tuple `e_j` by coordinatewise maximum.

Using `c_i = -1` and the standard basis tuples, express an arbitrary integer tuple `v` as a sum with nonnegative integer coefficients. State how to choose the common shift so every coefficient is allowed.
Check the representation coordinate by coordinate and conclude whether the three proposed starting tuples generate every integer-valued 2022-tuple.

Test the construction on a target having both positive and negative coordinates, explaining why a sufficiently large common shift still works. What upper bound on the minimum number of starting tuples follows?
For the lower bound, suppose there are only two starting tuples `v` and `w`. Show why universality is impossible if some coordinate has `v_i, w_i >= 0` or has `v_i, w_i <= 0`.

It remains to consider the case in which `v_i` and `w_i` are nonzero with the same sign at every coordinate. Use the pigeonhole principle to find two coordinates with the same sign pattern, then derive a fixed nonnegative ratio inequality preserved by both addition and coordinatewise maximum. Why does that prevent universality?
Combine the three-tuple construction with the obstruction for every pair of starting tuples, and determine the smallest possible value of `s`.
